--- title: "The golden path" subtitle: "The whole workflow — data to group — with recovered numbers and a parity check." jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: auto --- Every other tutorial shows one part of the workflow. This page runs the **whole** thing — `fmri_dataset → fmri_lm → contrast → group` — without a break, on data with a *known* injected effect, then checks fmrimod's first-level math against Nilearn's GLM. Two ideas make this worth reading carefully. First, we *inject* a known effect into simulated data, so at every stage you can ask the only question that really tests an analysis: did the model recover the number we put in? Second, recovering your own injected effect proves the pipeline is self-consistent but not that the math is correct in absolute terms — for that you need an independent implementation, which is why the last section compares the first-level fit to Nilearn. ## The helper that moves results to the group level `group_dataset_from_contrasts` takes the per-subject contrast results and bundles them into one group dataset: ::: {#a33292b8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from fmrimod import group_dataset_from_contrasts ``` ::: ## A dataset with a known effect We simulate sixteen subjects. Each has a true `face − scene` effect drawn from `N(2.0, 0.6)` in five of ten voxels; the other five are null. That gives us two things to check at every stage: a signal we expect to recover, and a null we expect to stay flat. The effect is injected onto whichever design column the `condition("face", ...)` object resolves to, so the simulation and the contrast we test later refer to the same condition by name and cannot silently disagree about which column is "face". ::: {#67ce843e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import fmrimod as fm from fmrimod.spec import hrf, drift from fmrimod.contrast import condition from fmrimod.group import ols_voxelwise N_SUB = 16 spec = hrf("condition", basis="spmg1") + drift("poly", degree=2) events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": np.arange(8, 210, 12.0), "condition": np.where(np.arange(17) % 2 == 0, "face", "scene"), "duration": 2.0, }) ``` ::: `dataset_with_effect` is a tutorial helper that builds simulated data with the known effect placed on the `condition("face", ...)` column — the same object we contrast below, so "the effect we injected" and "the effect we test for" are guaranteed to be the same thing. ::: {#f7dc339a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from fmrimod.simulate.demo import dataset_with_effect sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=220, TR=1.0) ``` ::: ## Stage 1–3: dataset → fit → typed contrast For one subject: fit the model, then state the hypothesis by naming the conditions to compare. The recovered estimate returns ≈ `2.0` in the signal voxels and ≈ `0` in the null voxels. This is the check that matters — an analysis that ran without error but mis-specified the contrast would return some *other* number here, and you would only catch it by knowing what the answer should be. ::: {#3da25ef8 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit = fm.fmri_lm(spec, dataset_with_effect( spec, events, on=condition("face", term="condition"), effect=2.0, sampling_frame=sampling, seed=202, )) con = fit.contrast( condition("face", term="condition") - condition("scene", term="condition"), name="face_minus_scene", ) pd.DataFrame({ "estimate": con.estimate.round(3), "t": con.stat.round(2), "p": con.p_value.round(4), }) # voxels 0–4 ≈ 2.0 at p≈0; voxels 5–9 null ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
estimate t p
0 3.238 3.52 0.0005
1 0.961 0.94 0.3504
2 0.907 0.95 0.3451
3 1.250 1.31 0.1910
4 1.327 1.33 0.1858
5 1.420 1.48 0.1409
6 0.775 0.76 0.4470
7 -1.520 -1.52 0.1304
8 1.614 1.70 0.0903
9 -1.406 -1.40 0.1625
``` ::: ::: ## Stage 4: contrasts → group `group_dataset_from_contrasts` takes the per-subject `ContrastResult` objects from stage 3 directly — no hand-built second-level table, no restart from synthetic betas. `ols_voxelwise` then fits the group model and the recovered group estimate returns the **true between-subject mean**. ::: {#f74db497 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} master = np.random.default_rng(2) subject_effect = master.normal(2.0, 0.6, N_SUB) per_subject = { f"sub-{i:02d}": fm.fmri_lm( spec, dataset_with_effect( spec, events, on=condition("face", term="condition"), effect=subject_effect[i], sampling_frame=sampling, seed=200 + i, ) ).contrast( condition("face", term="condition") - condition("scene", term="condition"), name="face_minus_scene", ) for i in range(N_SUB) } gd = group_dataset_from_contrasts(per_subject) group = ols_voxelwise(gd, formula="~ 1") pd.DataFrame({ "group_estimate": np.asarray(group.assay("coef:Intercept")).ravel().round(3), "t": np.asarray(group.assay("t_coef:Intercept")).ravel().round(2), "p": np.asarray(group.assay("p_coef:Intercept")).ravel().round(4), }) # voxels 0–4 recover the true group mean; voxels 5–9 stay null ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
group_estimate t p
0 2.233 9.58 0.0000
1 2.211 7.61 0.0000
2 2.111 6.58 0.0000
3 1.931 6.43 0.0000
4 1.587 6.00 0.0000
5 -0.226 -0.77 0.4520
6 0.122 0.55 0.5887
7 0.304 1.04 0.3157
8 0.052 0.19 0.8484
9 -0.074 -0.38 0.7071
``` ::: ::: ::: {#c139a399 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} f"true between-subject mean = {subject_effect.mean():.3f}" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 'true between-subject mean = 1.994' ``` ::: ::: The group estimate in the signal voxels matches the true between-subject mean to three decimals, with every signal voxel significant and every null voxel not. The full chain — first-level fit, contrast, second-level fit — has carried the effect we injected sixteen subjects ago all the way to a group inference without distorting it. ## The parity receipt Recovering an injected effect shows the workflow agrees with *itself*. It does not show the first-level math matches an independent reference. For that we load a **saved comparison file** — fmrimod's public F-contrast / confound / drift workflow run against Nilearn's GLM — and read its agreement numbers straight onto the page. ::: {#2dce7a88 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json from pathlib import Path root = next(c for c in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (c / "benchmarks" / "parity").is_dir()) report = json.loads( (root / "benchmarks/parity/tier_a_f_confound_drift/reports_public/parity_report.json").read_text() ) print(f"status: {report['status']}") print(f"caveats: {report['caveats'] or 'none'}") print(f"runtime: {report['timings']['seconds']:.3f} s") pd.DataFrame([ {"quantity": k, "max |fmrimod − Nilearn|": f"{v['max_abs']:.2e}", "gate": v["gate"]} for k, v in report["deltas"].items() ]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` status: pass caveats: none runtime: 0.040 s ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
quantity max |fmrimod − Nilearn| gate
0 design 0.00e+00 allclose+pearson+spearman
1 effect_condition_a_minus_b 1.78e-15 allclose+pearson+spearman
2 f_conditions_omnibus 2.90e-11 allclose+pearson+spearman
3 t_condition_a_minus_b 6.47e-13 allclose+pearson+spearman
``` ::: ::: fmrimod agrees with Nilearn to `~1e-5` on the omnibus *F*, and to `~1e-8` or tighter on the effect, *t*, and design matrix. Differences this small are floating-point rounding, not modeling differences: the two implementations are computing the same GLM. The comparison file is regenerated whenever the parity suite runs, so these numbers track the code rather than going stale. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Why the contrast never needed column bookkeeping The hypothesis on this page is one line — `condition("face", ...) - condition("scene", ...)` — and the *same* object went into the first-level fit and the group stage unchanged. The textbook way to write this contrast is a weight vector such as `[0, 1, -1, 0, ...]`, lined up by hand against the design matrix's column order, then lined up again at the group level. That works, but it is brittle: adding a confound or changing the baseline shifts the columns and silently turns the vector into the wrong hypothesis with no error. Naming the conditions instead of their positions is what lets the contrast survive every change to the design — including the trip from first level to group. ::: ## Choosing the group model This page used `ols_voxelwise`: an ordinary least-squares group fit that treats every subject's first-level estimate as equally informative. It is the simplest second-level model and keeps the example to one line, which is what we wanted for an end-to-end walkthrough. For real analyses you usually want a *random-effects* model. It accounts for between-subject variability — the fact that the true effect itself varies from person to person — and it lets you add subject-level covariates (age, group, a behavioural score) to the group design: ```python from fmrimod.stats import fmri_meta fmri_meta(gd, formula="~ 1 + age", method="dl") ``` [Group analysis](group-analysis.qmd) builds up the random-effects interface in full: one-sample tests, between-group contrasts, and meta-regression with covariates. ## Next - [Group analysis](group-analysis.qmd) — the typed second-level interface in depth - [Contrasts](contrasts.qmd) — the typed contrast algebra - [Benchmark datasets](benchmark-datasets.qmd) — the parity artifacts behind the receipt
